tagline: Alex Gordon & Jermaine Dye super collector · Kansas City Royals & Nebraska Cornhuskers team collector
intro: My name is Ian and my passion is collecting! Within this site you'll find thousands of high resolution scans of my cards (with a few game-used items as well). Every image is labeled with its database name. If you have a rare card of either player, have a Husker autograph I need, or see a card here you want to trade for, let me know!
_contactHelp: "contact.code" is my email address, reversed and base64-encoded so scrapers cannot read it; the site decodes it only when someone clicks. "contact.googleForm" connects the form on the page to my Google Form: "id" is the long code after /forms/d/e/ in the form's link, and each field is the form's "entry.123…" name for that question (from its pre-filled link). Leave "id" empty to use email buttons only.
_analyticsHelp: "analytics.goatcounter" is the site code from goatcounter.com (the part before .goatcounter.com). Empty means no analytics.

nflListStory: In the mid-2000s, I started a project to collect one autograph of every Nebraska Cornhusker to play in the NFL. I had no idea what an incredible journey that decision would start.

It began with picking up $5 autographed cards, which led to signed index cards for Huskers who never had a trading card. Years later, I made my first custom cards by designing them around some of those signed index cards. Eventually, I realized that no website had an accurate list of which Huskers actually played in the NFL; every one I found had errors or omissions. So I set out to build my own.

I have spent countless hours digging through old newspapers, media guides, college yearbooks and more to check every list I could find. The list featured here is the most accurate one available (so far!). What started as an autograph project has become the joy of researching, documenting, and now sharing Husker history.

dyeStory.title: Jermaine Dye: A Career in Cards
intro: I started collecting Jermaine Dye as a kid while listening to Royals games on the radio in the late 1990s. He flashed excellent power in the Royals big ballpark and had a cannon for an arm, winning a Gold Glove with the Royals in 2000. He, along with Johnny Damon and Carlos Beltran, formed one of the best Royals outfields of all-time. One wonders what the Royals could have been if they had been able to hold onto all three. Jermaine played for the Braves, Royals, Athletics, and finished his career with the White Sox, where he won World Series MVP in 2005.

I track my inventory of his cards with TradingCardDatabase as well as manually in Excel for stat generation. My primary focus of collecting is Game-Used relic cards, the rest I fill in when the price is right. I don't collect printing plates or other 1/1s unless they include an autograph or relic.

paragraphs: Jermaine is part of a select group of baseball players that have hit a home run in their first ever Major League at bat.

He connected for the notable blast on May 17th, 1996 against Marcus Moore of the Reds. He entered the game as a defensive replacement in the 5th inning, and then got his first turn to swing the bat in the 6th, where he made the most of his opportunity.

He made his mark in his first and only season with the Braves, playing a half season after replacing the injured David Justice and finishing 6th in the Rookie of the Year balloting. He stayed on with the team in the postseason, homering in the NLDS playoffs and helping the team make the World Series where they were eventually defeated by the Yankees.
Just before the start of the 1997 season, the Atlanta Braves traded Jermaine and a relief pitcher to the Royals in exchange for Keith Lockhart and Michael Tucker.
He struggled to stay healthy in '97 and '98, hitting well in AAA Omaha but struggling mightily with the big league club.

In 1999 it all came together, he was healthy for a full campaign and his hitting and fielding began to reach their potential. He slashed .294/.354/.526 and quickly became a fan favorite. The 2000 season was one of his finest efforts, as he hit .321/.390/.561 and earned the starting RF job for the American League All-Star team.

2001 was quieter from a performance standpoint, but he was still effective at the midway point in the season. Inexplicably, the Royals traded him in a three-team deal for the baseball disaster that was Neifi Perez, one of the worst trades in Royals history.

The Athletics were on the favorable end of the three team deal, and Jermaine quickly responded to the energy of a team in the thick of the playoff race. He improved every offensive and defensive statistic in the transition, and helped Oakland make the ALDS right before the start of the "Moneyball" era.
Unfortunately, injuries and slumps plagued him again and he struggled from 2002-2004 to maintain league average performance. At the conclusion of the '04 season, he hit free agency.

The White Sox signed Jermaine to a 2-year deal in 2005 and he began to return to form. He posted his best offensive numbers since '00 in his first campaign with the Sox and it culminated in a starring turn in the World Series. He hit an outstanding .438/.526/.688 with a home run, 3 runs batted in, and the clinching go ahead single in the final game to win World Series MVP.

He followed up with the best power output of his career in 2006. 44 HRs, 120 RBI, and a 1.006 OPS landed him an All-Star nod, a Silver Slugger, and a 5th Place finish in the AL MVP race, getting a 40% share of the vote.
He finished his career with the White Sox, announcing his retirement on March 31, 2011.

sections.title: About this site
sections.text: IanBadeer.com is a personal collection and research site, documenting players' careers through cards, autographs and memorabilia. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by any team, school, league or card manufacturer. Team names, logos and trademarks belong to their respective owners and are shown for identification and historical reference.

You may share and adapt them for non-commercial purposes with credit to Ian Badeer and a link to IanBadeer.com. News and media use with credit is welcome. Biographies adapted from Wikipedia stay under their own license ([CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)), and stats are from the sources credited where they appear.

sections.title: Card images & scans
sections.text: My custom card (ACEO) designs are © Ian Badeer; team logos and photos used in them belong to their owners. The card scans are images of cards in my collection; the original card designs belong to their manufacturers. Please don't reproduce, redistribute, hotlink, scrape or bulk-download these images, or use them in AI training datasets. Small thumbnails shown by search engines are fine.

_proballersHelp: ProBallers Player Unit widget on player bios (Ian's request). ids maps a player page slug to the number in that player's proballers.com address (proballers.com/basketball/player/NUMBER/name). A player with no id shows no widget.

signatures._help: Signature showcase (Ian's request): the signature's ink lifted out of one autograph scan on screen only (the scan file is untouched) and shown as a red neon sign. id = the card's Drive image ID; box = [left, top, width, height] as fractions of the scan; ar = the scan's width / height; ink = blue (default), dark (black marker) or both; src = a signature image Ian cleaned up himself (assets/signatures/), used instead of the scan; t = ink threshold (default 40, higher drops more background). Rules (Ian): show a signature only when it's complete and clean: nothing cut off by the sticker or crop edge, every loop whole, no streaky or broken strokes. No word inscriptions (e.g. '2001 Heisman'); a jersey number or a nickname is fine.

fanDay._help: Fan Day sheets (multi-signed, one box per player with his name printed under it): each player's box, cropped on screen only, on his page. id = the sheet's Drive image ID; box = [left, top, width, height] as fractions; ar = sheet width / height.
